text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game: keeping a token privately yields 1 point to self but costs others 0.75 each, while contributing to the group yields only 0.75 to self with the group's share split across members. I'm calculating what full cooperation versus full defection means for each player's total points.

Since private tokens dominate individually but group contribution maximizes collective welfare, this is a classic social dilemma. Given it's repeated over 10 rounds and I don't know how others will behave, I'll start cooperatively by contributing all 20 tokens to the group fund to signal good faith, then adjust based on how others respond.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This looks like a public goods game with a negative externality on private holdings. Keeping a token privately gives me +1 but costs others 0.75 each, totaling -2.25 to the group, while putting it in the group account gives me only 0.75 with no harm to others. So individually, keeping tokens private dominates, even though the group account is better for collective welfare.

Running the numbers: if everyone defects and keeps all 20 tokens, each ends up with 20 points. If everyone fully cooperates and puts all 20 into the group account, each ends up with 60 points instead. Given this is a repeated 10-round game, I'll open with full cooperation (contributing all 20 to the group) as a signal, and adjust my strategy based on how others respond in later rounds.

reply.thinking:
This looks like a public goods game with a negative externality on private keeping. I'm working out the payoff structure: each member keeps some tokens privately and contributes the rest to the group, where private tokens benefit the individual but impose a cost on others, while group contributions get multiplied and shared back equally.

Reading carefully, I think the group token pays only the contributor 0.75 points rather than being shared with the group, which makes private tokens individually dominant despite being socially worse overall. If everyone keeps all 20 tokens, each ends up with a lower total than if everyone contributed fully to the group, so I'm comparing the individual versus collective outcomes to confirm the free-rider dynamic.

Thinking about it more carefully, each token someone else keeps actually hurts my own payoff too, since their private holdings reduce everyone else's points by 0.75 per token. That means universal keeping is bad for all, yet without knowing individual contributions I can't enforce reciprocity—so I'm weighing whether to signal cooperation in round one despite the risk of being exploited.

I'm calculating what happens if everyone contributes fully to the group account versus keeping tokens private, to establish the social optimum.

Keeping tokens private is individually dominant since 1 > 0.75, even though it's worse for the group overall (full cooperation yields 60 per person versus 45 at baseline with pure defection). Since this is a repeated 10-round game, I'm thinking it makes sense to start by contributing cooperatively, perhaps putting all 20 tokens into the group account, and then adjust based on how others behave.

Now weighing whether to keep cooperating with another 20 contribution, versus keeping a token for myself—since each kept token nets me +0.25 personally even though it costs the group 0.75, I'm considering the tradeoff between short-term individual gain and collective payoff.

Defecting fully could net me 65 instead of 60 this round, but it would cut others' earnings and the total group fund would visibly drop, revealing cooperation broke down even if not who did it. With 10 rounds ahead and reputational signals mattering, I decide sustaining trust is worth more than a small immediate gain, so I'll stick with contributing 20.

With 10 rounds total, cooperation feels fragile but everyone benefits more from the 60-point outcome than the 45-point baseline, so I'll stick with contributing 20 again to keep signaling cooperative intent.
